concept.body: From one external point P, the two tangent segments to a circle are CONGRUENT (HL: shared hypotenuse OP, equal radius legs; then CPCTC). The figure O-T₁-P-T₂ is a kite with right angles at the tangency points, so angle P and the central angle are supplementary, and OP bisects both angles.

widget.prompt: One tangent segment from Q measures 9. The other tangent segment from Q = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 18 adds the pair — each segment individually measures 9.
4.5 halves — the congruence is a straight copy: 9.

steps.body: From any external point, exactly TWO tangent lines reach the circle — and their tangent segments are **congruent**: PT₁ = PT₂. Proof in one breath: triangles OT₁P and OT₂P share hypotenuse OP and have equal legs (radii), so HL congruence — then CPCTC hands over the tangent segments.

explanationVariants: The two-tangent theorem copies the length: PT₂ = 11.
HL + CPCTC: both tangent segments from P match, 11.

widget.prompt: From external point P, one tangent segment to the circle measures 11. The other tangent segment from P measures ?

commonErrors.feedback: 22 doubles — each segment is 11; it's the PAIR that's congruent, not summed: 11.
5.5 halves — the theorem copies, full strength: 11.

steps.body: Zoom out to the whole figure OT₁PT₂: two radii, two congruent tangent segments — **a kite**, straight from the quadrilateral course, with its right angles at T₁ and T₂. Its angle sum forces a clean supplement: **angle P + central angle T₁OT₂ = 180°**, since the two right angles spend the other 180.

explanationVariants: Quadrilateral sum 360, minus the two 90° tangency angles, leaves P + O = 180: central = 180 − 40 = 140°.
P and the central angle are supplements in the tangent kite: 140°.

widget.prompt: The two tangents from P meet at 40°. Find the central angle T₁OT₂ between the two radii.

commonErrors.feedback: 40° copies P — the kite's right angles force P and O to SUPPLEMENT: 180 − 40 = 140°.
50 = 90 − 40 complements — the pair shares 180° (the other 180 went to the two right angles): 140°.
320 = 360 − 40 charges P against the whole quadrilateral — the two 90°s already claimed 180: central = 140°.

steps.body: Two tangents from one point are always equal.

widget.prompt: Radius 6. Slide the outside point until each tangent measures 8, and watch the two tangents as you move.
widget.successFeedback: The point sits 10 from the centre. But look at what never changed: the two tangents were EQUAL at every position. They must be — the two right triangles share the hypotenuse (the centre-line) and have equal legs (the radii), so they are congruent. The two-tangent theorem is that congruence, nothing more.
widget.lowFeedback: Shorter than 8 — the point is too close to the circle.
widget.highFeedback: Longer than 8 — bring the point in toward the circle.

predict.prompt: As an external point moves, how do its two tangent lengths compare?

options.label: They alternate which one is longer

predict.reveal: The radii to the tangent points form congruent right triangles with a shared hypotenuse, forcing equal tangent segments.

cml.actionGoal: Move the external point while tangent lengths, radii, and right-triangle evidence update together.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Move the point farther from the circle. Which measurements change, and why does PA = PB remain true?

explanation.prompt: Why are the two tangent segments equal?

options.label: The two radius-tangent triangles are congruent by hypotenuse-leg.
options.feedback: They share the center-to-point hypotenuse and have equal radii as legs.

options.label: The drawing happens to look symmetric.
options.feedback: Appearance is not proof; right-triangle congruence supplies the guarantee.

options.label: Every tangent segment equals the diameter.
options.feedback: Tangent length changes with the external point and need not equal the diameter.

explanationVariants: OP is the kite's symmetry axis — it bisects angle P (and the central angle). Half of 40° is 20°.
The HL congruence already matched the half-angles at P: 20° each.

widget.prompt: Same figure, angle P = 40°. What angle does OP (the line from P to the center) make with EACH tangent?

commonErrors.feedback: 40° is the WHOLE angle at P — the symmetry axis OP splits it evenly: 20° per side.
70 = 140/2 halves the CENTRAL angle — that's the split at O. At P: 40/2 = 20°.
90° belongs at the tangency points — at P the axis bisects: 20°.

widget.prompt: A straight belt leaves a circular pulley. At the exact point where the belt lifts off the pulley, the belt is:

options.label: Tangent to the pulley — perpendicular to the radius at the lift-off point
options.feedback: A taut belt leaving a wheel runs along the tangent line — which is why belt-length problems are tangent-segment problems.

options.label: A chord of the pulley
options.feedback: A chord would CUT through the pulley — the belt hugs the outside and departs along the tangent.

options.label: Aimed at the pulley's center
options.feedback: Aimed at the center it would be a RADIUS direction — the belt leaves perpendicular to that: tangent.

options.label: At a random angle depending on tension
options.feedback: Any non-tangent angle would either cut the pulley or leave slack — taut geometry forces the tangent.

hints: Each external point owns a matched pair: from A both tangent segments are equal, likewise from B.
AT = 7 forces the other segment from A to be 7; the tangency point splits AB.
explanationVariants: From A: 7. So the shared tangency point splits AB into 7 + (from B) = 18, giving 11 — and B's OTHER tangent segment is also 11.
Two-tangent theorem at B copies its 18 − 7 = 11.

widget.prompt: Segment AB = 18 is tangent to a circle at a point between A and B, with the tangency point 7 from A. A second tangent is drawn from B. How long is B's tangent segment on that second line?

commonErrors.feedback: 7 is A's tangent length — B's runs from B to the tangency point: 18 − 7 = 11, copied to the second tangent by the theorem.
18 is all of AB — B only owns the part past the tangency point: 11.
9 halves AB — the tangency point sits at 7 from A, not the midpoint: B's share is 11.

widget.fallbackFeedback: B's tangent segment = 18 − 7 = 11; the two-tangent theorem copies it to the second line.

takeaways: PT₁ = PT₂ — HL on the radius triangles, CPCTC on the tangents.
OT₁PT₂ is a KITE: right angles at the touch points, so angle P + central = 180°, and OP bisects both.
Tangent segments chain: equal pairs at every external point.
steps.teaser: Next: a triangle wrapped around a circle — tangent pairs at every corner.
